epistemology.label: Historical epistemology
epistemology.description: Here the label denotes the French tradition associated with Bachelard and Canguilhem: histories of scientific concepts, norms, and discontinuities. It informs Foucault through a route distinct from structural linguistics. It is not an umbrella for every historical or sociological account of scientific knowledge. Bachelard’s own preliminary discourse distinguishes normative epistemology from a chronological history and calls its period labels approximate. Canguilhem’s norm/average discussion draws on Halbwachs and human geography; his later preface distinguishes newly encountered works from resources actually used in 1943.
epistemology.representative_figures_and_works: French history and philosophy of science; this connection prevents treating Foucault as merely a descendant of structural linguistics. Bachelard, La formation de l’esprit scientifique (1938); Canguilhem, the normal/pathological essay (1943; expanded 1966) and La formation du concept de réflexe (1955).

nationalismstudies.label: Nationalism studies
nationalismstudies.description: Makes the formation of nations and traditions an object of historical explanation. Anderson, Gellner, and Hobsbawm offer different modernist accounts; ethno-symbolist and postcolonial critics question their premises. Treating national identity as historical does not require assuming that every tradition is a recent invention.
nationalismstudies.representative_figures_and_works: Benedict Anderson, Imagined Communities (1983); Ernest Gellner, Nations and Nationalism (1983); Hobsbawm and Ranger, The Invention of Tradition (1983); Anthony D. Smith; Partha Chatterjee, Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986).

representative_people.context: Connects national imagining to print markets and language; imagined communities are not thereby unreal.
representative_people.works: Imagined Communities (1983)

representative_people.context: Relates nationalism to modern mobility and mastery of a shared literate culture; his reply to Smith allows varied cultural continuities.
representative_people.works: Nations and Nationalism (1983); Warwick reply (1995/1996)

nationalismstudies.scope_note: Anderson, Gellner, Hobsbawm, Smith, and Chatterjee supply competing accounts, not a common modernist theory. Hroch’s comparative phases, Billig’s everyday reminders and Yuval-Davis’s gender analysis address different questions. Nations, states and nationalist movements are not interchangeable; European typologies require testing beyond their original cases.

consumption.label: Consumption & material culture
consumption.description: Examines commercial promotion, household demand, goods’ changing value, taste, gender and provisioning. McKendrick, Brewer and Plumb distinguish commercial and social changes; de Vries connects consumption with household labor; Mintz links diets to colonial production. Anthropological and feminist approaches ask how objects acquire meanings and how consumer roles depend on unequal social relations.
consumption.representative_figures_and_works: McKendrick, Brewer, and Plumb, The Birth of a Consumer Society (1982); Appadurai, ed., The Social Life of Things (1986); Brewer and Porter, eds., Consumption and the World of Goods (1993); Mintz, Sweetness and Power (1985). Additional readings: Douglas and Isherwood, The World of Goods (1979); Kopytoff on cultural biography (1986); de Vries on industrious change (1994); de Grazia and Furlough, The Sex of Things (1996). Maxine Berg and Helen Clifford, eds.: Consumers and Luxury (1999).

consumption.scope_note: Demand, taste, provisioning, commodities, and material objects are not one theory; gender and empire connect consumption to production. Commodity circulation, cultural biography and goods as communication are distinct questions. De Vries acknowledges conflicting household interests; feminist research does not reduce women to consumers. Much of this selection concerns Europe and the United States; Mintz’s colonial production connects regions but does not make the coverage global in every respect.

strands.title: Commercialization and the consumer-revolution thesis
strands.focus: Fashion and pottery promotion, politics, leisure and childhood are different parts of the 1982 collaboration. Its consumer-revolution framing and gender assumptions invite criticism.
strands.works: The Birth of a Consumer Society (1982)

strands.title: Households, labor and demand
strands.focus: The industrious-revolution argument connects demand with household labor, including unequal interests and negotiation among members.
strands.works: “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” (1994)

strands.title: Commodity histories, labor and empire
strands.focus: Trace sugar from colonial slave production to changing diets and industrial work; consumption and production belong in the same historical question.

strands.title: Circulation and the politics of value
strands.focus: Following exchanged things connects valuation to social and political relations; Appadurai explicitly develops a resource from Simmel.
strands.works: The Social Life of Things (1986), introduction

strands.title: Cultural biographies and changing commodity status
strands.focus: A thing’s commodity status can change over time or differ between people; material production alone does not settle its social classification.

strands.title: Goods as social communication
strands.focus: Douglas and Isherwood examine goods as an information system through which people conduct social relations.

strands.title: Taste and social position
strands.focus: Read tastes and cultural practices in relation to social position, alongside approaches centered on circulation or household provisioning.

strands.title: Gendered consumption, work and identity
strands.focus: Investigate the division of family labor, male and female consumer identities, class differences and state definitions; avoid one universal consumer.

strands.title: Inventory evidence and its boundaries
strands.focus: Weatherill records selected goods across probate inventories. Missing laborers, debts, real estate and reliable clothing values constrain what household ownership can establish about society.

strands.title: Purchasing as household work
strands.focus: Vickery’s selected households distribute purchasing tasks and authority unevenly. Expenditure diaries show practical expertise, but incomplete income records limit reconstruction of financial power.
strands.works: The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998), “Elegance” opening and notes 15–18

strands.title: Material meanings and unequal possibilities
strands.focus: Vickery finds social ambition alongside attachment and remembrance. Age, resources and inheritance matter; her chapter does not establish one feminine attitude to possessions.

strands.title: Competing chronologies and questions
strands.focus: Compare McKendrick’s eighteenth-century acceleration, Weatherill’s earlier middling ownership and de Vries’s household labor argument. Vickery questions universal motives. Different evidence and outcomes do not yield one automatic date for a consumer society.
strands.works: McKendrick (1982), introduction; Weatherill (1996), preface; de Vries (1994); Vickery (1998)

strands.title: Ming consumers and social distinctions
strands.focus: Clunas reads Wen Zhenheng’s judgments about appropriate objects as elite distinctions, then compares them with Yan Song’s confiscation inventory. These are different sources, not interchangeable records of actual purchasing.

strands.title: Whose consumption becomes visible?
strands.focus: Clunas’s selected texts privilege elite men. Rules assigning objects to women do not directly recover women’s own meanings; subsistence consumers also remain poorly represented. Pagani highlights this limit while praising the method.

strands.title: Relics and changing value
strands.focus: Geary follows transfers and renewed authentication of relics. Their careers may change how communities value them; price equivalences and the relative frequency of different transfers remain uncertain.

strands.title: Specific historical uses of theory
strands.focus: Vickery explicitly uses Bourdieu and Douglas/Isherwood; Geary cites Kopytoff. These establish particular uses with different evidence and questions, without proving uniform reception across consumption history.

strands.title: Luxury and European consumer culture
strands.focus: Berg and Clifford coedit a volume on luxury and consumer culture in Europe, 1650–1850. This records their editorial contribution; detailed chapter arguments remain unchecked.

daniel_k_richter.description: A historian of early North America who reconstructs colonial encounters from the standpoint of Native communities. edges.relationship: Haraway contributes a feminist argument for situated and accountable scientific objectivity
edges.evidence_note: Scoped to feminist science studies within the gender-history entry; does not represent all gender historians.

edges.relationship: Labrousse supervises Perrot’s strike research, which adapts serial training to workers’ lives
edges.evidence_note: Lacoue-Labarthe’s scholarly biography identifies thesis supervision and statistical training alongside voices and gestures. This names one formation and selective adaptation; Perrot’s later feminist programme is not reduced to this connection.

edges.relationship: Fox-Genovese defends narrative interpretation and challenges Stone’s assumptions about crisis and progress
edges.evidence_note: Her December 1978 letter explicitly states that Tuchman does not subscribe to Marxism. This is a supportive critical intervention in reception, not an influence on the completed book or endorsement of every conclusion; Stone’s reply remains visible in the same source.

edges.relationship: Smith-Rosenberg contributes to Spiegel’s social and textual method
edges.evidence_note: Romancing the Past introduction note 7 cites The Body Politic and thanks Smith-Rosenberg for a draft; acknowledgments credit sustained exchange and her reading every chapter. This is a concrete reciprocal contribution, not gender history receiving theory only from outside.

edges.relationship: Perrot: serial training and strike histories
edges.evidence_note: Retrospective biographical evidence documents supervision and a particular adaptation; Perrot’s later feminist work is not reduced to this training.
edges.map_label: Perrot: serial training and strike histories

edges.relationship: Partha Chatterjee’s 1993 intervention challenges Anderson’s modular derivation of colonized nationalisms and foregrounds autonomous cultural imagining in colonial Bengal.
edges.evidence_note: Specifically named critic, primary The Nation and Its Fragments pp. 4–7 freshly reread in rotated scan/OCR. Chatterjee acknowledges the print-capitalism insight while contesting derivative national models; material/spiritual distinction remains his historically situated claim.

edges.relationship: Examines how tastes and classificatory judgments relate to social position and struggles over legitimacy.
edges.evidence_note: Retained selected primary transcription presented as selections from pp. 466–484 of Nice’s 1984 translation, not the entire printed conclusion or book. No new statistical check, field-wide reception or universal class law.

edges.relationship: Nancy Fraser challenges the exclusionary assumptions of the bourgeois-public model and distinguishes counterpublics and decision-making publics.
edges.evidence_note: Incoming edge locates Fraser’s specifically named 1990 intervention, not a consensus of gender historians. Reuses retained selected pp. 56–62, 67, 75–77 and stated fragments/notes. Note 9 acknowledges Habermas knew alternative publics; counterpublics can themselves exclude.

edges.relationship: Doreen Massey’s 1995 intervention disputes Harvey’s treatment of tradition and the political possibilities of place.
edges.evidence_note: Incoming edge locates Massey’s individually named criticism, not a group consensus. Retained complete-article OCR review, with missing words and no complete textual collation; Harvey pp. 302–304 separately visually checked. Old collective arrows remain.

edges.relationship: Supplies Canguilhem with a specifically acknowledged statistical criticism of the abstract average human being.
edges.evidence_note: Named Canguilhem reception from retained Norme et moyenne selection and bibliography item 53. Halbwachs’s 1912 original remains unread. This does not substitute his collective-memory books for the statistical intervention or certify medical/racial historical examples as present facts.

edges.relationship: Criticizes colonial land restriction as a means of making people dependent on wage labour.
edges.evidence_note: Own Capital I chapter 33 opening and colonial-land discussion read. This is a specific criticism of Wakefield; Mill is not named in this passage, and no direct Marx-to-Mill attack or complete Indigenous history is inferred.

edges.relationship: Links nationalism to modern mobility and mastery of a shared literate culture maintained through political and educational institutions.
edges.evidence_note: Retained primary Gellner reply, with newly inspected central paragraphs on mobility/high culture and contingent continuities. These are his explanatory claims, not a universal outcome or an assertion that cultures lacked any earlier political expression.

edges.relationship: Questions an account of discipline centred on the apparatus that produces it
edges.evidence_note: General Introduction xiv–xv directly discusses Discipline and Punish and asks how users appropriate or evade disciplinary arrangements. This specific criticism preserves the acknowledged analytical debt.

edges.relationship: Questions the uniqueness and uniformity of European family patterns
edges.evidence_note: Primary 8–9 distinguishes kinship questions from demographic measures, stresses regional/social variation and considers Tibet/Roman Egypt counterexamples. The cited studies themselves were not independently checked.

prior_scope.geographic_emphasis: Primarily Western academic historiography, with selected independent and critical traditions.
notes: Dates describe approximate emergence or expansion, not termination.
Edges are selective teaching interpretations, not an exhaustive genealogy.
Connections may express influence, overlap, conceptual resources, or critique; read each relationship label.
A node’s source is a supporting reference and does not necessarily document every associated edge.
Nodes include traditions, fields, genres, methods, approaches, and individual thinkers.
New and revised relationships may include source_ids and evidence_note. A comparative teaching link does not assert influence merely because it has a source and target.
Editorial revision 1.3 incorporates selected and rewritten Fable 5.1 proposals into the existing revision 1.2; the supplied feedback used an older base and its edge IDs were remapped.

Schema 1.2 adds optional edge directed and relationship_kind fields. Explicit comparisons have directed:false; missing direction metadata on inherited edges means not yet classified, not verified influence. Critique arrows point from critic to the position criticized.

Optional source citation and verification fields distinguish bibliographic identity or supporting-page checks from an unperformed passage-level audit. Missing verification metadata means unrecorded, never implicitly verified. Checked metadata does not certify all node or edge interpretations.

The map remains selective: a named work, school, or field does not imply that every associated thinker agrees. Paired nodes such as Progressive/consensus history are comparisons, not single paradigms.

Revision 1.4 distinguishes women as producers of historical knowledge from women’s history as a field. Women historians appear across economic, political, military, intellectual, and other inquiries; belonging to the profession does not imply a shared feminist method or a linear succession of feminist waves.

Schema 1.3 adds shared people records, explicit group/person entry kinds, and qualified representative_people rosters. Roster inclusion is not a new influence edge or a claim of formal school membership. Most rosters normalize existing curated prose; their inherited references are not new individual affiliation verification.

Directional neighborhood views place incoming directed relationships on the left and outgoing ones on the right. Comparisons and unclassified links sit separately. Thompson’s cultural contribution and feminist historians’ productive inheritance coexist with their criticisms; no uniform succession from class to culture is implied.

From revision 1.133 the atlas has no closing date. Fields are extended one at a time; each entry states the year through which it has been reviewed. The original 1920–2000 experiment (revision 1.121) is kept as an archived view.

frame.note: Open frame from revision 1.133. Each entry records how far it has been reviewed (coverage.reviewed_through); a review year is a limit of our reading, not an ending.
